title: A few words: the sambutan
title_target: Yang terhormat, Bapak dan Ibu sekalian
goal: Write and deliver a *sambutan* — the short formal address that opens every Indonesian event — with its fixed running order: salutations by rank, the greeting, *puji syukur*, the message, and the closing formulas. Short in the middle is fine; short at the edges is not.
bekal: open a formal address in the right order: *Yang terhormat…, yang saya hormati…, Bapak dan Ibu sekalian*
choose a greeting that suits a mixed audience: *Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua*
close with the standard formulas: *Demikian yang dapat saya sampaikan…*, *Mohon maaf apabila…*, *Terima kasih atas perhatiannya*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Menyusun sambutan
dialogs.intro: Late July. In a week the first forty Program Jembatan students fly to Australia for a semester, returning in December, and Sarah must give the director's address at the send-off. She has emailed Pak Hendra her draft; he calls her into his office.

notes: **Sambutan, pidato, ceramah.** A *sambutan* (from *sambut*, to welcome) is the short address given by an official or host at an event, often several in a row. A *pidato* is any speech; a *ceramah* is a lecture or sermon. At a wedding or an inauguration you will sit through three or four *sambutan* before anything happens, and nobody minds.

**Rank order is protocol, not etiquette.** Big events have a *protokol* officer whose job includes the list of VIP guests in order. Naming a minister after a deputy is noticed. If in doubt, ask the organiser for *susunan tamu VIP* and read the names exactly as written, titles included.

**The multi-faith greeting.** The long *salam lintas agama* spread through government events as a gesture of inclusion. In 2024 the Indonesian Ulema Council advised Muslims not to use it, since it includes other faiths' religious greetings, and practice now varies. Pak Hendra's advice is the safe one: the neutral *salam sejahtera bagi kita semua* works for any audience.

**Rahmat-Nya.** Pronouns referring to God are capitalised and hyphenated in standard spelling: *rahmat-Nya* (His grace), *kepada-Mu* (to You), *Engkau*. It is one of the EYD rules even Indonesians check, and a sambutan script is exactly where it gets checked.

**Tuhan Yang Maha Esa** — “God the One and Only” — comes from the first principle of Pancasila and is deliberately neutral among the recognised religions. That is why it, and not *Allah* or *Tuhan Yesus*, appears in public speeches. *Maha* is a Sanskrit-derived intensifier: *Maha Esa* (written apart before *esa*), *Mahakuasa*, *mahasiswa*.

**Basa-basi** is small talk and ritual politeness — asking *Sudah makan?*, praising the host's house, the long opening of a speech. English speakers often call it “beating about the bush”; Indonesians call skipping it *kurang sopan*. Pak Hendra's point is that the opening is not filler but the part that shows respect.

grammars.title: The running order of a sambutan
body: Almost every sambutan, from a village head's to a minister's, follows the same seven steps. Only step 5 is truly yours; the rest are formulas the audience expects to hear.

head: Step
Typical formula
Notes
rows: *Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.*
*Puji syukur kita panjatkan ke hadirat Tuhan Yang Maha Esa…*

after: Step 5 is where Sarah's Australian instinct is an asset: Indonesians sit through many sambutan and are grateful for one whose message fits into two minutes. Keep the frame, trim the middle.
*Pada kesempatan yang berbahagia ini* (“on this happy occasion”) is the classic bridge into the message. *Pada kesempatan ini* alone is fine for a less festive event.

grammars.title: Yang terhormat, yang saya hormati, yang saya banggakan
body: The salutations climb down a ladder. Each rung has its own phrase, and the phrase comes before the title and name, never after the whole list.

head: Phrase
For whom
Example
rows: the most senior guests, one by one
*Bapak dan Ibu sekalian yang saya hormati*

after: ⚠️ The abbreviation *Yth.* belongs on envelopes and letters only. Out loud it is always *Yang terhormat* in full.
Notice the MC says *kami hormati*, the speaker *saya hormati*: the MC speaks for the organisers, the speaker for himself or herself.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Hari pelepasan
dialogs.intro: The send-off, a week later, in a university auditorium in Depok. Fajar, surprisingly polished in batik, is the master of ceremonies; forty students in matching jackets sit in the front rows.

notes: **Waktu dan tempat kami persilakan** — literally “time and place we invite (you to)” — is the MC's fixed formula for handing over the floor. The structure is *Kepada [person], waktu dan tempat kami persilakan.* No other wording sounds right, so don't improvise.

**The audience answers back.** Indonesian audiences return a greeting in chorus, and a speaker who hears a weak reply may try again: *Kok lemas? Selamat pagi!* Students are drilled in enthusiastic answers — *Luar biasa!*, *Siap!* — from primary school, and they perform them with gusto.

**Adik-adik** — “younger siblings” — is how an adult addresses young people in a speech: warm, slightly teacherly, never condescending. Sarah then switches to *kalian*, the natural plural “you” for a younger group. For adults she would have said *Bapak dan Ibu*.

**Duta bangsa** (ambassadors of the nation) and **Jagalah nama baik…** (guard the good name of…) are the heart of every Indonesian send-off. The *-lah* on *jagalah* turns a plain command into a solemn exhortation, the register of speeches and sermons.

**A joke in a sambutan** is allowed if it is short and at your own expense. *Rupanya mikrofonnya ikut gugup* (“it seems the microphone had nerves too”) laughs at the situation and at the speaker, never at a guest. *Rupanya* — “it turns out” — is a good friend for this kind of dry aside.

**Kata-kata yang kurang berkenan** — words that were “less than pleasing” — is the ritual apology that closes most speeches. Nobody believes you have offended anyone; saying it shows humility. *Berkenan* also means “to be willing” in polite requests: *Apakah Bapak berkenan hadir?*

grammars.title: The ceremonial -lah and the MC's formulas
body: Ceremonies have their own grammar: commands softened into exhortations with *-lah*, invitations with *marilah*, and passives that keep the organisers politely in the background.

head: Formula
English
Where
rows: Let's give a round of applause…

after: ⚠️ *Bukan hanya… melainkan juga…* is the standard pattern for “not only… but also”. After *bukan* the standard contrast word is *melainkan*; *tetapi* follows *tidak*: *bukan pelajar, melainkan guru* but *tidak mahal, tetapi enak*. Speakers mix them constantly, but a scripted sambutan should not.

blocks.text: Indonesia recognises six religions, and each has its own opening and closing greeting. At an event for one community, use theirs; at a mixed or official event, the neutral form is always correct.

head: Audience
Opening
Closing
rows: *Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.*

blocks.text: A non-Muslim speaker who opens with *Assalamualaikum* at a Muslim event will usually be received warmly; just make sure you can pronounce it and the reply, *Waalaikumsalam*, when the audience answers. When unsure of your audience, stay neutral.
A good close strings three or four of these together. They are so fixed that the audience will often start applauding at *Demikian*.

blocks.title: A ninety-second sambutan skeleton
items: *Yang terhormat [top guest], yang saya hormati [others], Bapak dan Ibu sekalian.*
*Selamat pagi dan salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.*
*Puji syukur kita panjatkan ke hadirat Tuhan Yang Maha Esa… Terima kasih kepada [hosts] atas [what].*
*Pada kesempatan yang berbahagia ini, saya ingin menyampaikan…* (two or three sentences)
*Semoga… Demikian yang dapat saya sampaikan. Mohon maaf… Terima kasih atas perhatiannya.*
